newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany set to stress commitment to strong mark.
newsitem.headline: Germany set to stress commitment to strong mark.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government on Wednesday is set to launch the next stage in Germany's battle to defend the symbol of its postwar prosperity and tell markets it wants a strong deutschemark.
The government is likely to comment on recent foreign exchange developments at a regular news conference at 1230 GMT, government sources told Reuters.

The sources said the cabinet, which began meeting at 0730 GMT, would probably not conclude a formal statement of its own but that Finance Minister Theo Waigel would discuss the issues with cabinet ministers.
"No formal statement is expected," one government source said when asked about the cabinet meeting.

Any statement by the government would mark the next phase in Germany's battle to assure financial markets that it wants the mark to enter European monetary union as a strong currency and the it wants the euro to be as strong as the mark.

Waigel led the charge on Tuesday, saying the recent weakening of what has been a rock solid currency for nearly half a century was an overreaction of financial markets concerned about European monetary union.

Waigel's rare foray on to the foreign exchange battlefield caused the dollar to stumble temporarily, but the U.S. currency quickly regained its footing and in the evening Waigel renwed his warnings and set the stage for the next attack.
Speaking in the southern town of Dillingen late on Tuesday, he said: "Wait until tomorrow. The cabinet will make a statement on this."

He had said earlier in Berlin that markets had overreacted in pushing the dollar and sterling to multiple-year highs, and hinted that the Group of Seven rich industrialised nations could be prepared to take corrective action.

Waigel's support for the mark came hot on the heels of similar statements from Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer last week but failed to hold the dollar back as it soared to 71-month highs above 1.80 marks.

The G7 industrialised nations, which in 1995 called for an "orderly reversal" of the dollar from record lows near 1.3450 marks, signalled in February when the dollar rate was about 1.65 marks that the recovery had gone about far enough.

Analysts have blamed the mark's weakness on a row in Germany over how strictly entry criteria for European economic and monetary union (EMU) should be interpreted. They said this has discredited both the planned euro and the mark itself.
Bundesbank council member Franz-Christoph Zeitler, also speaking late on Tuesday, said the mark's appreciation against other currencies may have become somewhat excessive.

"The appreciation of the deutschemark has been corrected in the meantime and that may even go somewhat beyond a correction," Zeitler told a regional business seminar in Bavaria. He did not specify what exchange rates he was referring to in regard to the mark's movements.
The mark's weakness comes at a critical point for Germany, with the planned launch of the European single currency now less than 18 months away.

Tietmeyer in his comments made the point that it was essential that the mark go into the joint currency from a position of strength. Strategic use of a weak currency to promote trade is anathema to inflation-conscious Germans.

But in a vicious circle of economic argument, wrangling over the precise fiscal criteria for monetary union -- and the various accounting methods one could adopt to reach them -- has damaged the credibility of the euro, and of the mark.
Economists said the current currency situation no longer reflected the strength of the dollar or of sterling, but the weakness of the mark.
